claims.text: Catalytic performance in ethanol oxidation is governed by in-situ formation of a transient surface oxide such as PtOx.
The transient surface oxide is dynamically generated under electrochemical potential cycling.
The oxide layer modulates adsorption of ethanol and its intermediates.
Dynamic surface oxidation suppresses catalyst poisoning.
Dynamic surface oxidation selectively promotes the 12-electron/12-proton ethanol-oxidation pathway.
Suppression of poisoning and promotion of the 12-electron/12-proton pathway enhance catalytic activity and durability.
The catalyst begins with a pristine or lightly oxidized surface.
Cycling between approximately 0.5 and 1.0 V versus RHE is the proposed controlled change, with constant-potential operation as the comparator.
Potential cycling repeatedly forms and reduces a thin PtOx surface layer.
Repeated oxide formation and reduction dynamically restructure the catalyst surface and alter adsorption energies.
Constant-potential operation does not favor dynamic oxide modulation.
Constant-potential operation may cause greater poisoning or product overoxidation.
Optimized potential cycling will produce higher ethanol-oxidation current density than constant-potential operation.
Optimized potential cycling will improve product selectivity and durability relative to constant-potential operation.
Minimal dynamic surface-oxide formation is expected under the constant-potential baseline.
The proposed mechanism applies under moderate potential cycling in aqueous ethanol oxidation near ambient temperature.
An excessively wide cycling window can lead to excessive oxide buildup and invalidate the proposed beneficial mechanism.
The mechanism may fail in substantially different media or under extreme potential or pH conditions.
Particle size and catalyst-support effects may also influence ethanol-oxidation performance.
